# A Short Summary
## of this Book:

High and deep foundations concerning the **Threefold Life of Man** through the <term>Three Principles</term><note>A central concept in the philosophy of Jacob Böhme, referring to three realms of reality: the dark fire-world (source of power/wrath), the light-world (divine love), and the visible world (our physical reality).</note>, in which is clearly shown both the **Eternal** and the **Mortal**: And why **God** (the <term>Highest Good</term><note>Often referred to in Latin as the *Summum Bonum*, the ultimate source of all happiness and virtue.</note>) has brought everything forth into the **Light**: Why also one thing runs against another and corrupts it: And then / what may be **True** or **False**, and how the one separates from the other: Wherein primarily the **Three Principles** are grounded / which are then the sole origin or source from which all things flow. 

Wherefrom also may be clearly recognized the manifold **Opinions of Faith** / why and from what cause so many various opinions arise among the <note>original: "Menschen-Kindern," literally "children of men," a common biblical expression for all of humanity.</note> **Children of Men** concerning the **Essence** or the **Will of God** / and what is also necessary and useful for man to do, so that he may become a partaker of the **Highest** or **Eternal Good**: And then also at the same time concerning the outcome and end of all things / [where]<note>The text ends mid-sentence at the catchword "war," which likely continues as "warumb" (why) or "waren" (were/was) on the next page.</note>

can be seen in all fires. For life draws its sustenance <note>original: "Zehrung," meaning the fuel or consumption required to keep a fire burning.</note> from the body, and the body from its food; for if the body no longer has food, then the fire of life consumes it, so that it withers and perishes, like a meadow flower that falls over if it has no water.

<margin>4. There is a life in man that is eternal, namely the soul</margin>
4. But since there is yet another life in man that is eternal and unbreakable, namely the soul, which is also a fire, and yet must have sustenance just as the mortal life does, we must therefore contemplate its source <term>Quall: a central concept in Böhme’s work, describing the "welling up" or "source-spirit" of life which can be both a source (Quelle) and a torment (Qual).</term> and its food—what it is that gives it food forever, so that it is never extinguished in eternity.

<margin>Perception of the soul's hunger for the Highest Good, the Divine Life</margin>
5. And thirdly, we find in our soul-life that there is still a great hunger within it for another higher and better life, namely for the Highest Good, which is called the Divine Life; so that the soul does not let itself be satisfied with its own food <note>Böhme suggests the soul has its own natural "fire-food" but craves a higher "divine-food."</note>, but desires with great yearning and longing the highest and best good, not only for a delight, but, in its hunger, as a food.

<margin>True knowledge, that every life desires its mother as a food</margin>
6. Thus we have, in great wisdom and true knowledge, the understanding that every life desires its mother—from whom that life is born—for its food. Just as wood is the mother of fire, so the fire desires it, and if it is separated from its mother, it is extinguished. Likewise, the earth is the mother of all trees and herbs; they desire her. And water, along with the other elements, is the mother of the earth; otherwise, they would remain in death, and neither metal nor trees, nor any herb or grass, would grow in or out of her.

<margin>The life of the elements is a boiling; when this stops, the elemental warmth is extinguished.</margin>

8. Since it is then eternal, it must also come from the eternal, as the dear Moses writes quite rightly of it: God breathed the living breath into man, and so man became a living soul.

<margin>God is everything, and yet no thing is God: He dwells within Himself, in another principle.</margin>
9. We cannot say, however, that because man exists in a threefold life, each life stands separately with a distinct form. Rather, we find that they are within one another, and yet each life has its effect in its own <term>domain: "Regiment," referring to a governing sphere or realm of influence.</term>, as if in its mother. For just as God the Father is everything—since everything <term>originates: "uhrständet," meaning to arise or take its stand from a primal source.</term> from Him—and is present in all places and is the fullness of all things, yet the thing does not grasp Him. Nor is the thing God, neither of His Spirit nor of the true Divine Essence <note>original: "Göttlichen Wesens."</note>. One cannot say of any tangible thing: "This is God," or "God is here more than in other places." Yet He is truly present; He holds the thing, but the thing does not hold Him, for He does not dwell in the thing, but in Himself, in another <term>principle: "Principio," the Latin term for a beginning or fundamental source.</term>

<margin>The soul dwells in the body and is surrounded by the stars and elements.</margin>
10. Thus also is the soul of man breathed in by God; it dwells in the body and is surrounded by the spirit of the stars and elements, not

# Of the Threefold Life Ch. 2.

The ground is laid out: that in the beginning, as in the <term>center: *Centro*</term>, was the eternal Word, and the Word was God’s, and the eternal will is that same Word. For the eternal God has that same will within himself, and it is his heart; and in that same <term>re-focused: *wiedergefasseten*</term> <note>This refers to the divine will grasping or forming itself into a distinct presence.</note> will in the eternal Father of all things, the <term>Godhead: *Gottheit*</term> has its name **GOD** <note>original: *GOTT*</note>.

7. For we cannot say that God has a maker; thus the will also has no maker, for it always makes itself from eternity; and yet it is not a "making," but an eternal birth; the Word in the Father, and the Spirit, which goes forth in the <term>power: *Krafft*</term>, is the life of the Godhead.

8. ### Chapter 2. Of Man.

The first will is not called God, but <term>Nature: *Natura*</term>; the second will is called <term>Alpha and Omega: *A und O*</term>, the Beginning and the End, from eternity to eternity. And in the first will, Nature would not be manifest; the second makes it manifest, for it is the <term>power: *Krafft*</term> within the strength, and without the one, the other would be nothing.

10. Since the Father's will is the first in eternity, he is also the first person in the <term>Trinity: *Dreyzahl*</term>, being the <term>center: *Centrum*</term> itself. Thus, this is the will or center: namely, the <term>desire: *begehren*</term> to give birth to the Word or <term>Heart: *Hertze*</term>. For otherwise there is nothing, nor may anything be named earlier than the desire within the will.

For in the whole <term>Abyss: *Tieffe*</term>, there would otherwise be nothing and nothing would appear; instead, all would be eternally still.

# Of the Threefold Life Chapter 2.

**Freedom** outside of nature is **God the Father**, and nature is born within Him in such a way that He is an Almighty Ruler over nature, just as the human **Mind** <term>*Gemühte*: the deep seat of the soul, will, and disposition</term> is over the senses: For everything has an **origin** <note>original: *Uhrkundt*; meaning a primal source or original record</note>, as we intend to show you hereafter.

27. Also, the lightning goes straight through the **sting of fury** of the **turning wheel**, where then the sting must give way on both sides, and the lightning drives through the middle: Thus from the **wheel** a **cross** is made, and it can no longer turn, but stands trembling in the sharp power of the **will** of **eternal freedom**, which is God the Father.

28. ### Chapter 2. Of Man. <note>original: *Cap. 2. des Menschen.*</note>

The will is [driven] to fly out from and above the four forms <note>the "four forms" refer to the four lower qualities of nature—contraction, expansion, rotation, and fire—which Böhme describes as the foundation of material existence</note>, above nature itself, and to ignite nature within the fire—and thus to become a more terrifying power, as can be conceived in the devils who live in this will, as we shall set forth hereafter.

38. Therefore, understand us correctly [regarding] what the ancient sages <note>likely referring to Hermetic philosophers and alchemists</note> understood by these three words: **Sulfur**, **Mercury**, and **Salt** <note>original: *Sulphur, Mercurius und Sal*</note>. Although they were not able to grasp the high Light entirely, they nevertheless had a sufficient understanding of it within the light of this world, namely in the third **Principle** <note>original: *Principio*; the Third Principle is Böhme's term for the visible, material universe</note>, which has the same meaning and concept throughout—except that they did not understand the [other] Principles; otherwise, they would have recognized God. Thus, they remained as heathens in the light of this world with their understanding. For they discovered the soul of the four forms in the power of the sun, but the second Principle <note>the "Second Principle" is the world of Light and Divine Love</note> was not further revealed to them.

39. This was hidden from them, as indeed it is even today; but time reveals it, as it stands as a banner <note>or standard-bearer</note>, whereof we shall speak in its proper place.

40. ### Concerning the seventh form of Eternal Nature / the open gates of the Being of all beings.

29. My dear reader, if you wish to understand the high mysteries, you do not first need to set an Academy <note>original: "Academiã"; Böhme is criticizing the reliance on formal university education over spiritual experience.</note> upon your nose, nor use a pair of spectacles, nor read the books of many masters; for they are not to be sought, found, or grounded solely in the high schools <note>refers to universities.</note>. 30. Seek only the Word and Heart of God—which became human—in the manger by the ox in the stable, in the dark night. **49.** Since all creatures exist within the Father, and for this reason he is called Father—as the Father of all beings—and we humans are also his children; yet, alongside Adam, we have strayed from the power of the seventh spirit of the Word. Through our imagination <note>To Böhme, "Imagination" is the creative power of the mind to "form" itself into a specific spiritual state.</note>, we have turned toward the "out-birth" of the Father—that is, the spirit of this world—which clothes us in perishable flesh and blood and holds us captive within itself. For we are the image of the Godhead, in which the Spirit of God reveals His wonders. And let yourselves be rightly advised: God the Father has reborn us in Christ, so that we should, with our imagination, enter again into the Word—into the center of His heart flaming with light—so that the Holy Spirit might once more proceed out from us with powers, wonders, and deeds, as was seen in the humanity of Christ.

58. The soul has not been torn away from the Father’s **essences** <note>original: "Essentien"</note> / as if it were no longer within the seven spirits of nature: No, that cannot be / Everything stands within the seven spirits of the Father’s nature / even the Heart of God itself / only the seals of death in the **fierceness** <note>original: "Grimme." In Böhme’s writing, this refers to the harsh, wrathful, or 'dark' quality of nature before it is enlightened by Love.</note> are broken and opened by the Light in the Heart of God in the **Center** <note>original: "Centro"</note> of the human soul.

59. For that we thank God the Father / in Christ Jesus / who became Man / and gave us **rebirth** <note>original: "Wieder-gebuhrt"</note> into the Light in Him / and redeemed us from the dark, fierce torment in the zeal of wrath for eternity.

60. But because we humans did not recognize such great grace and light / and did not respect it / but instead allowed ourselves to still love Adam’s flesh / and the lust of this world / even though we clearly saw how God performed great wonders and deeds in Christ the **man** / <unclear>as well as after him, in his disciples,</unclear> and all who clung to him with earnestness in the new rebirth / instead we pushed away our own lamp / and lived in hypocrisy / in our own **dissimulation** <note>original: "Gleißnerey" — a term for false piety or outward shows of holiness</note> / in tyranny / and persecuted Christ / so He also left us sealed / so that we did not recognize His light / but instead sought our own ways to God / and wanted to reach God through our own delusion / the kingdom of this world was dearer to us than God’s kingdom / we practiced only hypocrisy before Him / and our heart was far from Him. Thus we must also remain under the seals in the Father’s nature / until the spirit **Mercurius** <note>original: "Mercurius." For Böhme, this represents the active, "working" power of nature and the spirit that drives transformation.</note> has displayed all his wonders in us.

<summary>Böhme explains that the soul remains part of God's natural essences but is spiritually liberated through Christ, though he warns that humanity often rejects this grace through hypocrisy and worldly desire.</summary>

# Chapter 4.

## Concerning the seventh property of nature, the essence or corporeality. Also: Concerning the three Persons in the Deity.

1. 2. # Chapter 4. Of the Threefold Life.

...retains the other / and even though they now stand within one another in six forms / yet there is no place of rest / but there is a constant desire of all six forms / like a **hunger** / from which the **Will** is then always born: and since there is nothing / where rest might be / except for the **still Eternity** / and yet such rest cannot be grasped or found in the **wheel of the fiery essences**; <note>The "fiery wheel" or "wheel of nature" is Böhme’s term for the first four properties of existence—harshness, bitter sting, anguish, and fire—which churn restlessly until they find the light.</note> so hungry Nature seeks in her mother / namely in the desire of **harshness** / <term>Herbigkeit: Also known as astringency or tartness. 9. # Chapter 4. Of Man.

In Böhme's thought, even spiritual realities have a "body" or substance.</term>

### The mightiest portal in the Center, to be highly considered.

13. We show this to you in Light and Darkness: For we cannot say that the Darkness is the **agony** <note>original: "Quahl". For the Darkness has no desire, but the desire is born within it, and the Darkness causes the desire, so that a desire arises—as if to be **free** from the Darkness.

14. sink: and the sharpness of the Fire-Flash <term>Fewer-Blitz: In Böhme's cosmology, this is the sudden, lightning-like ignition where the dark, contracting forces of nature are transformed into the light of spirit.</term> in the sharp Freedom retains its right, as a still agony, which stands in the sharpness of Freedom. And the sinking of the anguish is to be compared to a death, out of which life is born: and this same death gives weight; for against the Fire of Freedom it is like a sinking into oneself, and in its sinking, the anguish becomes material, so that in this death the entire form of the agony is made graspable—or sensitive, as I might say—and this sensitivity is the loveliness of the Darkness, and the Fire of Freedom in the fierce flash is its spirit and life; and it is hereby indicated to you that you should go into yourselves, and see that the fire creates feeling in the sharpness of the dead corporeality: for without fire, no body has any feeling: as you see this in the earth and stones.

Now it is further shown to you, that the body or the substantiality <term>Wesenheit: A term used by Böhme to describe the "being-ness" or essential substance of a thing, bridging the gap between spirit and matter.</term> is not a death in such a way that it is worthless, or merely a useless thing; for the suffocation <note>original: "Erstickung". 16. # Of the Threefold Life Chapter 4.

<margin>
Chapter 4 of the 3rd [book].
God’s will in a self-conceived will arising from fierce pride envies a Divine Heart.
God is not recognized in pride.
The <term>tincture</term> <note>the vital spiritual essence that gives life its quality</note> becomes false and retreats into the lower center.
All doing out of one's own nature—where humility is not in God’s love and does not do God’s will—is wickedness and not divine; nor is it born in God.
The soul must be born in God if it is to do God’s will, for then it is an heir of God and of the Son, Christ: and does what God wills and not its own nature. Even if it performs the works of nature, they are in God, for its will is in God.
The soul's doing is born in God.
Nature's doing is conceived in the soul.
The son is a servant <note>Böhme suggests that while the spirit/son is free, the outward actions of nature remain a "servant" or secondary result</note>.
</margin>

...held as the source-well of their own nature, and have ignited the <term>Matrix</term> <note>original: "Matrix"; the generative "womb" or fundamental environment of nature</note> of fierceness, wrath, and envy: This is now their eternal delight.

43. The <term>tincture</term> <note>spiritual essence</note> has become false in their self-conceived will, in which they wished to rule over the humility of God’s Heart out of fierce pride; and for that reason, they were cast out from the upper <term>Center</term> <note>original Latin: "Centro"</note> into the lower one, as a dead thing, where there is nothing but vanity and darkness, and they cannot reach the Light of God.

44. For the Light of God requires a disposition of humility, in which the desire of Love is born, which takes hold of the Heart of God. And this is not in Lucifer, but rather mere wrath, envy, and pride—always wanting to fly out above the Heart of God and to rule in stern power. Therefore, he has been cast out of the Divine <term>Principle</term> <note>original Latin: "Principio"</note> into the <term>Center</term> <note>original Latin: "Centrum"</note> of darkness; that is his eternal kingdom.

45. And it is clearly shown here to those theologians who presume to preach of God’s will, that their fictions regarding the ways to God are but fables, where laws are made in order to reach the Kingdom of God. It stands alone in this, and depends on our <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "imagination"; the creative power of the will to shape its own spiritual reality</note>, that we draw our will into humility, within which Love is born—which presses toward the Heart of God as its own property—where then the human soul is born in God, so that it receives God’s will, to do what God’s will is.

### Chapter 4. Of Man.

...[without] God’s will, is only a carved work <note>original: "Schnitzwerck"; Böhme uses this to describe man-made intellectual or religious constructs that lack divine life</note> of natural artifice, which remains in the anguish of the Center <note>the fundamental driving forces of nature that produce conflict and desire</note>, and is a seeking where nothing is; like one who makes an artistic work in which he takes pleasure; so also do such works stand before God as a figure, which indeed remain in that figure for eternity.

47. <margin>Center</margin>
48. As we have then clearly indicated to you, how all being is born out of the will, and everything has its reproduction in the will. 49. Thus the origin of nature has the second <term>Principle</term> <note>original Latin: "Principium"</note>, out of which now come beings that may be changed; but the <term>Principle</term> <note>original Latin: "Principium"</note> of the Heart of God cannot be changed.

50. Therefore I say again, and it is the precious truth: everything that is carved out and taught concerning the way to God—if it does not lead to the gentleness <note>original: "Sanfftmuht"</note> of love and further into the grasping of the will toward the Heart of God—then it is all only a—

<header>Of the Threefold Life, Chap. 4. 96</header>

<margin>
Chap. 4. The Son is the Father’s Light / and is a Word / that He speaks out from the essences in the **Center of Nature** as a way or will of God. [He] is a Word / an image of eternity / a light / in which nature is light / and is the Father’s eternity in God / who forms Himself into the Word of Love / and is yet in the Center of Wrath / acting as a victory over the wrath / wherewith God the Father is full of joy. <unclear>...</unclear>

...all according to whether he conceives something good or evil within himself / as **Reason** <note>original: "Vernunfft"; Böhme often uses this to describe the human intellectual capacity which must choose between the impulses of the light and dark worlds.</note> will decide: So it is also in the Father within Nature / but not in the **Freedom** <note>original: "Freyheit"; Böhme's term for the "Unground" or the absolute state of God that exists before and beyond all created nature and manifestation.</note> : for there, within itself, is nothing but the luminous eternity.

66. Thus, since two kinds of conception proceed from one **Will** / such as toward joy and sorrow / toward love and enmity / so each has its own birth toward opposition <note>original: "Wieder-willen"; literally "against-will" or "antagonism." 67. **Nature** has its will toward the sharpness of the strict birth / and the first will of the Father / which originates out of the luminous eternity / [tends] toward still **Gentleness** <note>original: "Sanfftmuht"; this is Böhme's primary term for the Second Principle—the cooling, loving, and soothing quality of the Light that balances the Fire of the first principle.</note> / just as the still eternity is a still, gentle delight without substance in itself ; thus there are two kinds of drive in one being / and also two Centers are born therefrom ; one hastens toward gentleness / and the other toward **Wrath** <note>original: "Grimm"; representing the foundational, consuming fire and "severity" of God's first principle, which provides the energy for existence.</note> / and yet they are not separated / for the wrath in nature is the first / and out of the eternal wrath the gentleness is born / that is the second / and one would be nothing without the other / but only a still eternity.

68. ### Of the Threefold Life, Chapter 4

As your being and property <note>original: "Wesen/und Eigenthumb"; refers to one's inherent essence and the specific qualities that belong to one's nature.</note> are, so also is the eternal birth in God: for God is Spirit, and your internal governance <note>original: "Regiment"; the ruling principle or spiritual direction within the body.</note> in your body is also spirit, and it has gone forth and been created out of God's governance.

76. For God has revealed Himself in the human spirit, both in love and in wrath: both <term>centers</term> <note>original: "Centra"; the focal points or "hearts" of spiritual activity.</note> are within it, and the third, together with the outgoing of the spirit, is Omnipotence—provided that the spirit of this world, as the third <term>principle</term> <note>original: "Principium"; Böhme’s term for the three fundamental layers of reality: the dark fire, the light, and the physical world.</note> in *Adam*, had not placed its bolt <note>original: "Riegel"; a bar or obstruction.</note> therein. This bolt broke the birth of *Christ* <note>original: "Christi"</note> and turned it into a wonder <note>original: "Wunder"; here meaning a miraculous sign or a mystery to be gazed upon.</note>, where it is now displayed before God as a great wonder.

77. In the same way, we also recognize the third Person of the Deity, who goes forth from the Father and the Son: for He is the Spirit of the Mouth of God, and He does not have His <term>origin</term> <note>original: "uhrstandt"; the primordial source or "original standing."</note> in Nature, but He is the Spirit of the first Will in Nature. However, He receives His sharpness <note>original: "Schärffe"; the active, defining power that allows a spirit to act upon matter.</note> in Nature, and therefore He is the Shaper and Framer <note>original: "Formner und Bilder"</note> in Nature, acting as one mighty and omnipotent.

78. For He carries the sword of omnipotence: He is the Bringer-forth <note>original: "Gebährer"; the one who gives birth to or manifests life.</note>, the Director, the Guide, and the Breaker of wickedness, and the one who unlocks hidden things. He originates Himself in the Father from eternity without beginning: for without Him, the Father was nothing but an eternal stillness, without being <note>original: "Wesen"; essence or tangible reality.</note>.

79. He is the essence of the will, just as has been mentioned regarding the fire, out of which the air originates, which goes forth from the fire.

Of the Threefold Life Chapter 5.

# Chapter V.
## Of the precious and highly noble Virgin of the Wisdom of God, and of the Angelic World. To be highly regarded as the second gate into the Holy Ternary <note>original: "Ternarium Sanctum"; Böhme uses this Latin term to describe the "holy ternary" or the manifested spiritual realm of the Trinity.</note>.

1. I know that the sophist <note>Böhme frequently uses "sophist" to refer to the university-trained scholars and theologians who relied on intellectual logic and literalism rather than spiritual experience.</note> will charge me with pride for this—that I, a lowly and humble man in this world, should climb so deep into these mysteries. But let it be said to you: you stand upon the wisdom of this world, which I regard as nothing, for it gives me no joy. But I rejoice in this: that my soul floats in the wonders of God to His praise, so that I may recognize His miraculous work, in which my soul delights as if in its mother. Thus every spirit speaks of its mother, from whose food it eats, and in whose source-spirit <note>original: "Quahl"; Böhme uses this word not in the modern sense of "agony," but to mean the fundamental quality, source-spring, or essential nature of a thing.</note> it lives.

2. Since I now recognize these wonders, should I then remain silent? For I was born for this very purpose—as were all creatures—that they should reveal God's wonders. So now I work in what is mine, and another works in what is theirs, and you, proud sophist, also work in what is yours.

3. We all stand in the field of God and grow toward God’s miraculous work and glory—the godless as well as the pious—but every plant grows in its own quality <note>original: "Quahl"</note>. When the reaper comes to mow them down, each will enter into its own...

For he is pulled by two: by the Spirit of God and by the Devil, in whose bonds he also remains caught according to the outer, sinful man; and his center stands directly upon the **cross** <note>The original uses the symbol †</note>, and in this world he is like a scale, where now one side is up, now the other is down; and here we are only in the vale of tears, in anxiety and need.

31. Since God is then so near to us—indeed, is within our very selves—let us seek Him: and if we then wish to find Him, we must turn back from this world and become as an uncomprehending child that only clings to its mother, and be *born anew* in God, in sense and mind. Otherwise we cannot see Him, as Christ Himself teaches us, so that His Light may shine within us.

32. We must completely exit our reason and not look upon the deceptive art of this world; it is of no use to us for this Light, but is only a wandering and a restraint.

34. Understand it rightly: in the holy number of three—not in the Majesty, which is without essence, but in the distinction of the Trinity, where the Godhead is called Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is where the two *Principles* <term>Principia: the two foundational forces of reality—God's love/light and God's wrath/fire</term> separate, the holy and the wrathful. There, the lightning flash makes a ☩, and upon the ☩ the Heart of God is born. It stands as a heart in the body, or as a Word of God the Father in His *center* <note>original: "Centro"</note>, and thus makes another center within itself; for it enters into itself, even into the light of the Father’s freedom.

...distinguished, recognized in the Light before the Majesty. Understand the meaning correctly:

102. Just as the mouth forms the word **Created** <note>original: *Schuff*, the archaic past tense of the German *schaffen* (to create). **45.** Understand us correctly, how this world is in its foundation: The eternal center of life’s birth and of the essence is everywhere: When you enclose a small circle, like a small grain, the whole birth of eternal nature is therein, and also the three-fold number in the <term>Holy Ternary</term> <note>original: "Ternario Sancto". # Chap. 6. Of Man.

<margin>

**46.** When I pick something up and carry it away, I do not carry eternity away, much less God; and yet eternity is indeed in that thing. However, the thing is an **out-birth** <note>original: "außgebohren". This is a key term for Böhme, referring to the physical world as something "born out" of the spiritual realm.</note> and it stirs eternity, but the "out-born" thing cannot grasp or contain eternity. Yet eternity grasps the "out-born" through and through, without moving: For eternity, along with the Godhead, is in one place just as much as in another; for within it there is no "place," rather it is the manifestation <note>original: "Aufgebuhrt". Literally an "up-birthing" or the act of coming into existence.</note> that creates place and location. Therefore God says: **I am the Alpha and Omega, the Beginning and the End.** <note>original: "Ich bin A und O". Böhme uses the German letters A and O to represent the Greek Alpha and Omega from Revelation, signifying God's all-encompassing nature.</note>

**47.** This world creates a beginning, and God in the **Number 3** <note>original: "3. Zahl". A reference to the Holy Trinity.</note> is that beginning; it also creates an end, which is eternity, and that is also God: For before this world, only God existed from eternity. But the reason we do not grasp this is that in God there is no "grasping" or "concept" <note>original: "Begriff". This word implies both a mental concept and a physical containment or boundary.</note>; for wherever there is a concept/boundary, there is a beginning and an end. Therefore we are enclosed in darkness so that we might labor and manifest God, just as we have shown regarding the **seven forms of nature** <term>seven forms of nature</term> <note>In Böhme’s complex cosmology, these are seven "qualities" or "spirits" (such as contraction, expansion, and heat) that interact to bring the hidden God into visible manifestation.</note>, which perform an eternal labor within themselves, so that one form gives birth to another until they are all brought to the **Light**. In this way, the Eternal stands revealed in a **threefold form**, which otherwise would not be known.

**48.** We show you this: that the eternal essence is like a **human**, and this world is also like a **human**: Eternity gives birth to nothing other than its own likeness, for there is nothing else within it, and it is unchangeable. If it were not, it would pass away or become something else, which is impossible.

He concludes that both the eternal essence and the physical world are structured in the likeness of a human being.</summary>

# Of the Threefold Life Chap. 6.

**49.** Just as you now see and perceive that man is, so also is eternity: Consider him in body and soul, in good and evil, in joy and sorrow, in light and darkness, in power and im-potence, in life and death. Heaven, earth, stones, and the elements are all within man, as is the **Number 3** <note>original: "drey Zahl". A recurring term for the Holy Trinity in Böhme's cosmology.</note> of the Godhead; nothing can be named that is not in man. All creatures are in man, both in this world and in the **angelic world** <note>original: "Englischen Welt". In 17th-century German, "englisch" refers to angels, not the English nation or language.</note>; we are altogether, with the whole essence of all essences, but one body in many members, where each member is itself a whole, and each member has its own particular task.

**50.** O man! seek yourself, and you shall find yourself; see, your whole being consists of **three principles** <note>original: "drey Principia". Böhme’s core doctrine of the three "worlds" or realms that coexist: the dark fire-world, the light-world, and the outer physical world.</note>, where none exists without the other; they do not stand beside one another, or above one another, but within one another as one, and they are indeed but one, yet according to creation they are three. You may ask: how is this? Adam's soul was from the eternal will, from the **Center of Nature** <note>original: "Centro Naturæ". A Latin term Böhme uses to describe the dynamic point where spiritual energy begins to manifest from the abyss.</note>, from the **Cross** <note>represented by the symbol "+" in the text.</note> of the Number 3, where light and darkness part. Understand this: it was not a divided spark, like a piece of the whole, for it is no piece, but rather the whole; just as the whole exists in every single point. Now the eternal Center creates the eternal **essence** <note>original: "Wesenheit". This refers to the substantial or "bodily" aspect of the spirit, the "stuff" of the spiritual realm.</note>, acting as a sinking and a rising, from which the movement of the **element** <note>original: "Elements" (singular). Böhme often speaks of the one "pure element" of the spiritual world from which the four worldly elements are derived.</note> arises, as well as the penetrating and multiplying; though there is nothing there but such a spirit, yet the essence is the body and an **im-potence** <note>original: "un-macht". Here used to mean a lack of active force, representing the passive, receptive nature of substance/body compared to the active, "powerful" spirit.</note>, for it is a sinking, while the rising is the spirit.

<meta>catchword: 51. Thus</meta>

<summary>Böhme explains that man is a microcosm containing all aspects of reality, including the Trinity and the angelic world. He describes the soul's origin in the "Center of Nature" where spirit and substance (essence) interact through a process of rising and sinking.</summary>

### Chapter 6. Of Man.

56. Now the image—that is, man—stands in the middle, between the **Kingdom of God** and the **Kingdom of Hell**, between love and wrath. Whichever spirit he gives himself over to, that is the one he belongs to. Even if man plunges himself into wrath, nothing is lost from the Godhead. For the first "breathing-in" <note>Referring to the divine breath of life in Genesis 2:7.</note>—which is the Spirit of God himself—has its own **Principle** <term>Principium: In Böhme's thought, a "Principle" is a fundamental realm of existence, such as the Light-world or the Dark-world.</term> and is not seized by the wrath. It is as if the **Trinity** <note>original: "drey Zahl", literally "three-number."</note> dwells in the midst of the wrath, and yet the wrath does not disturb it, nor even know it; there is no feeling or seeing between them. For the image awakens the source-torment of wrath, and the first breathed-in spirit within that image flares up in the grimness of **pride**—all according to how he has built his character during this life. Yet, the original divine form loses nothing, for that torment is not truly within that [divine] image; rather, the image withdraws into its own Principle along with the beautiful **Maiden of Wisdom** <note>original: "Junckfrawen der Weißheit". For Böhme, Sophia or Divine Wisdom is a celestial mirror and companion to the soul.</note>, and the human image is transformed into a **serpent’s image**. For as the spirit is, so too is the body: into whatever "will" the spirit takes flight, it shapes its body into that same form and source of torment.

57. Thus we know that everything has come from a single fountain, and the tangible essence of this world had a beginning; therefore, it is also a "death." For whatever is not from eternity is mortal.

58. However, so that the human image (which, in its body, also had a beginning) might endure, **GOD became man** and dwells again within the soul. Thus, the soul has once more attained that first image which exists outside of this world—but only for those who give themselves over to **GOD**,

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 6 regarding the nature of the human soul and its relationship to the Divine. Having previously distinguished the soul from the Word (the second person of the Trinity), Böhme now employs one of his most famous metaphors—the glowing iron—to illustrate how the human and the divine can coexist without losing their individual essences.</meta>

### Chap. 6. Of Man.
<meta>catchword: 90. God</meta>

<margin>An earthly parable of the glowing iron.</margin>
84. I give this earthly parable: Look at a glowing iron, which in itself is dark and black; and the fire penetrates the iron, so that it all shines.

<margin>The iron and the fire remain unmixed together in their own properties.</margin>
85. Now, nothing actually happens to the iron; it remains iron, and the <term>source-torment</term> <note>original: Quahl; a key term for Böhme, punning on "Qual" (torment/pain) and "Quelle" (source/wellspring), referring to the intense, vibratory energy of life</note> of the fire retains its own right. It does not take the iron into itself, but rather it penetrates the iron; and the iron is as free in itself at one time as at another, and so too is the source-torment of the fire; neither one becomes the other.

<margin>The soul in the fire of the Godhead.</margin>
86. In this way, the soul is set into the fire of the Godhead; the Godhead shines through the soul and dwells in the soul, but the soul does not grasp the Godhead; rather, the Godhead grasps the soul, and yet does not transform it, but only gives it the divine source-torment of <term>Majesty</term> <note>The light-world or the glorious presence of God</note>.

<margin>Meaning of the source-torment, radiance, and proceeding.</margin>
87. If the soul now appropriates itself within the divine <term>source-well</term> <note>original: Quälle</note>, then it remains in the Majesty of God; for the source-torment signifies the Word, and the radiance signifies the Majesty, and the proceeding forth from the source-torment—like the heat from the iron—signifies the Holy Spirit.

<margin>How the glowing iron is extinguished in water.</margin>
88. If the glowing iron is now thrown or falls into water, then the fire’s source-torment, radiance, and the proceeding of the heat are all extinguished at once:

<margin>How it went for Adam when he turned away from God.</margin>
89. This is also how it went for Adam: he threw himself out of God’s Majesty with his will into the spirit of this world; thus he went out from God. God did not extinguish within him like the glow of the iron—no, that cannot be, for He shines eternally.

<summary>Böhme uses the metaphor of glowing iron to explain how the human soul is permeated by God's presence without losing its individual identity, and how Adam's Fall was a turning away from this divine light into the spirit of the physical world.</summary>
<keywords>parable of glowing iron, soul and Godhead, source-torment, divine majesty, the Fall of Adam, Holy Spirit, nature of the soul</keywords>

# Of the Threefold Life, Chapter 6.

<margin>90. If Adam had remained in God, God would have enlightened him.</margin>
God remained in His <term>Principle</term> <note>original: *Principio*; Böhme uses this to refer to the fundamental source or "ground" of existence</note>, and Adam went out; had Adam's will remained in God, it would have been known, and God would have remained in the will; thus the <term>Majesty</term> <note>The divine light and glory of the second "principle" or the Kingdom of Heaven</note> would have illuminated the will.

<margin>91. As Adam went out from God, this world, death, the devil, and hell caught him.</margin>
91. So he went out from the will of God into this world; thus this world caught him—as did death, the devil, and hell—and they dwelt within Adam.

<margin>92. Not only God's Spirit, but also the elements breathed into man: however, if he had remained in God, the element would not have captured him. 2nd Part in the Philosophical Questions.</margin>
92. Adam was in this world; he lived in the elements, and God also blew the air into his nostrils; but he was not to set his will therein, nor eat of earthly fruit which makes earthly flesh: that was his fall, that he ate of earthly fruit. Thus his <term>essences</term> <note>The inner spiritual qualities or "being-ness" of a creature</note> also became earthly, and the soul was captured by the earthly kingdom.

<margin>93. Adam hid himself from the Lord: he was ashamed when he was naked.</margin>
93. Then the <term>Word of the Lord</term> <note>original: *Verbum Domini*</note> spoke to the soul: Adam, where are you? And his body hid itself, so greatly was the poor soul ashamed; and Adam spoke: I am naked. The precious <term>Heavenly Virgin</term> <note>Sophia, or Divine Wisdom, who Böhme believes was the soul's original "garment" or companion before the Fall</note>, which was his garment, was lost; and the light of Majesty was lost, and Adam stood outside the Word.

<margin>94. Ah God! Ah God! How lamentable it is for a soul in the Fall! This imprisonment is miserable; God became man to lead us back.</margin>
94. Oh, this is terrible to the one who recognizes it! The soul trembles at it, and rightly fears this imprisonment, when the poor soul is to be captured by the devil and bathe in God's wrath; and that is the cause why God became man: that He might lead us back into the <term>Holy Ternary</term> <note>original: *Ternarium Sanctum*; Böhme's term for the holy, manifested realm of God's glory</note>, into the Angelic world.

<margin>95. Just as in Adam we all inherited death, so in Christ we inherited life.</margin>
95. And as we all have gone out from God with Adam (for we all have Adam's soul and flesh), so God has reborn us all in Christ.

<summary>Böhme describes the Fall of Adam as a shift in the human will from the divine Principle to the earthly world, resulting in the loss of the soul's divine "garment" (the Heavenly Virgin). He explains that the Incarnation of Christ was necessary to lead humanity back from this earthly imprisonment into the Holy Ternary.</summary>

## The VII. Chapter.

### How we must seek again that which was lost, etc.

<margin><unclear>Ch. 7.</unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear>The Lost</unclear></margin>

To US human beings in this world, it is of the greatest importance that we seek again that which was lost <note>This refers to the "Pearl" or the divine image of God within man that Böhme believes was lost during the Fall of Adam</note>. It helps nothing to prattle / that you know how to speak much of **God** / and yet you despise the simple-hearted / as the hypocrites upon the **Antichrist’s beast** <note>In Böhme’s time, the "Antichrist" and his "beast" (from the Book of Revelation) were frequently used to describe the corrupt institutional church or rigid religious authorities who persecuted spiritual seekers.</note> do / who forbid the light to those who see / as has also happened to this hand <note>original: *dieser Handt*; Böhme frequently refers to himself as "this hand" or "this pen," signaling that he considers himself a humble instrument of divine revelation.</note>. It is as **Christ** speaks: *Unless you turn / and become as children / otherwise you will not see the kingdom of heaven eternally* <note>original: "Es sey dann daß ihr umbkehret / und werdet als die Kinder..." paraphrasing Matthew 18:3.</note>: You must be born anew / if you want to see the kingdom of **God**; that is the right aim.

8. There is no need for art or eloquence for this / you need neither books nor art for it / a **shepherd** <note>Böhme emphasizes that a simple laborer—like himself, a cobbler—is as capable of divine insight as a scholar.</note> is as fit for it as a **Doctor** / and often much better: For he goes sooner out of his own **reason** <note>original: *Vernunfft*; Böhme views human "reason" as a limited tool of the physical world that often blocks spiritual "understanding."</note> into **God’s mercy**: He does not have great, wise reason / therefore he does not deliberate with it / but goes simply with the **poor tax collector** <note>A reference to the Parable of the Pharisee and the Tax Collector (Luke 18:9-14), where the humble sinner is justified over the prideful religious leader.</note> into the **Temple of Christ** / whereas the highly-learned man still first sets an **Academy on his nose** <note>original: *eine Academiam auff die Nasen setzet*; a vivid idiom suggesting that the scholar puts on his intellectual prestige or "scholarly spectacles" which actually distort his spiritual vision.</note> / and first considers / in what opinion he wishes to enter the **Temple of Christ**. He first adopts a human opinion / you want to seek **God** out of this or that opinion: One in the **Pope’s** opinion / the second in **Luther’s** / the third in **Calvin’s** / the fourth in **Schwenckfeldt’s** <note>Caspar Schwenckfeld (1489–1561) was a German theologian and mystic whose followers were often persecuted alongside other "Radical Reformation" groups.</note> / and so forth / there is no end to the opinions.

9. Thus the poor soul stands outside the **Temple of Christ** in doubt / knocks and seeks / and yet always doubts that it is not on the right way.

<summary>Böhme argues that spiritual truth is found through simple, childlike faith and internal rebirth rather than through scholarly "art," academic status, or the conflicting "opinions" of religious denominations like those of Luther or Calvin.</summary>

18. <term>Reason</term><note>original: *Vernunfft*. Böhme often personifies Reason as the limited human intellect that tries to understand divine mysteries through logic alone, often failing to see the spiritual truth.</note> says: if this world is harmful to man, why then did God place man in it? Now they have placed their will into their essences, and their will is eternal. Just as the <term>Center of Nature</term><note>original: *Centrū naturæ*. This refers to the core generative forces or "fountains" within both the spiritual and material world.</note> of the harsh <term>Matrix</term><note>original: *Matricæ*. A Latin term Böhme uses to describe the "womb" or generative source of nature from which all forms emerge.</note> is eternal, into which their will has gone; so they are only eternal spirits therein, also serving as a mirror for the other angels, as well as for the souls of men.

This can mean "essence," "being," or "substance."</note>, and thus into the time of the forms of nature.

### Chapter 7. Of Man.

[The Fa]ther’s nature [moved] toward the creation of the angels, and onward to this world. Secondly, the nature of the Son moves, where the Heart of God became man; and this shall not happen again in eternity. And even if it does happen, it happens through that same single (Man), for God is through many and in many. Thirdly, at the end of the world, the nature of the Holy Spirit will move, when the world shall return into the **Ether** and the dead shall rise. Thus the Holy Spirit will be the Mover; he will place all the great wonders that occurred in this world into eternal being, for God’s honor and miraculous deeds, and for the joy of all creatures. And he will be the sole Mover of the creatures—both angels and men—for through him **Paradise**, which we lost here, shall bloom again. Therefore know that the great wonders of the world, which were destined to pass away, stand before us.

23. This world is a great wonder; and would it ever have been recognized by the angels within the wisdom of God? Therefore, the Father’s nature moved toward the creation of being, so that the great wonders might be revealed; and then they will be recognized in eternity by angels and men, seeing all that was contained within His power. And the image of the number Three—as the eternal **Virgin**<note>The "Eternal Virgin" or Sophia is a central concept in Böhme’s thought, representing Divine Wisdom as a mirror or a passive, feminine principle through which God’s wonders are revealed.</note>, who stood in the <term>Holy Ternary</term><note>original: *Ternario Sancto*. A Latin term Böhme uses to describe the holy realm of the Trinity, often associated with the "divine corporality" or the spiritual environment of heaven.</note>, in the eternal wisdom, in the essence, as a figure—would never have been recognized by the angels in eternity if the **Heart of God** had not become man. There the angels saw the radiance of Majesty in a living image, in which the whole <term>Trinity</term><note>original: *Dreyzahl*. Literally "three-number," referring to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> was enclosed.

<summary>Böhme describes three divine "movements" (Creation, Incarnation, and Resurrection) that reveal God's hidden wonders to angels and humans. He emphasizes that the Incarnation was necessary for the angels to truly perceive the divine Majesty and the "Eternal Virgin" of Wisdom.</summary>

<keywords>Holy Spirit, Creation, Resurrection, Paradise, Eternal Virgin, Holy Ternary, Trinity, Incarnation, Divine Wisdom</keywords>

# Of the Threefold Life Chapter 7.

24. Thus, the <term>Center of Nature</term><note>original: *Centrum naturæ*. In Böhme’s cosmology, this refers to the inner, driving "wheel" or core of natural life and its forces.</note> would never have been revealed to the angels in all eternity—much less the dominion of the Holy Spirit—if this world with the stars and elements had not been created. Therefore, the angels recognize the eternal being with all its forms through this world, and so do we humans. For this reason, God created the image of the <term>Third Number</term><note>original: *Bildnuß der dritten Zahl*. This refers to Man as the representation of the "Third Principle"—the external, physical world which completes the manifestation of the Trinity.</note>, namely man, into this world, so that he should reveal all wonders and recognize the eternal God.

25. But the image became infatuated with it <note>original: *vergaffete sich*. To be dazzled or "gapingly" captivated by something, leading to a loss of spiritual focus.</note> and "imagined" into it, just as Lucifer did into the wrathful <term>Matrix of Nature</term><note>original: *grimme matricem Naturæ*. The harsh, dark, and unrefined root of nature that exists before it is transformed by divine light.</note>; thus was man also captured. For Adam was meant to be a lord over the stars and elements; nothing was to affect him; he was all-powerful; he could have moved mountains with a single word; he was a lord over fire, air, water, and earth, for there was no death in him. He was in **Paradise**; Paradisiacal fruit grew for him. He was one person, and not two; he was both man and woman, and was meant to give birth to an angelic kingdom from within himself. And that was possible, for he did not have such flesh and blood as he had after the Fall, when he was ashamed of it before the Majesty of God. He had flesh and blood, but it was heavenly; his <term>essences</term><note>original: *Essentien*. The spiritual-material "virtues" or substances that constitute a being's inner nature.</note> were holy. He could give birth without the tearing of his body to an image like himself. For he was a **virgin**, without the female form, after the shape of the Eternal [Virgin], with a pure, luminous mind, and moreover chaste without [carnal] desire. His desire was only [to produce] his like out of himself—

# Of the Threefold Life Chapter 7.

...driven, and the **Word of the Lord** <note>original Latin: "Verbum Domini"</note> presented itself with a promise of the **Serpent-crusher** <note>original: "Schlangen-treter"; a reference to the Messiah who, according to Genesis 3:15, would bruise the head of the serpent.</note> into the Light of their life, which previously dwelt in them and ruled in them. That now remains in its **Principle** <note>original Latin: "Principio"; Böhme uses "Principles" to describe the fundamental layers of reality: the dark world, the light world, and the material world.</note>, and the image remains in the outer **Principle**, and was captured by the astral and elemental spirit. The governance of this world now dwelt alone in these humans, and they became earthly. Then God cursed the earth for man's sake, so that no more Paradisiacal fruit grew. Everything was lost, except for God’s grace and mercy, which still remained.

For they now stood with the world's foundation in the abyss of hell among all the devils, and lived in powerlessness, as we still do today; they fathered children in two realms, for the wrath of God had now captured them and wanted to manifest its wonders in them. Likewise, the **Serpent-crusher** had also captured them into the Light of life and wanted to manifest his wonders in them as well. There arose strife and unrest, as can be seen in their children; the first born of woman was a godless murderer who desired to suppress God's kingdom, and the other was a holy, pious man. In short, you see it in all of Holy Scripture, especially with *Cain* and *Abel*, and with *Isaac* and *Ishmael*, and also with *Esau* and *Jacob*, who even in the mother's womb quarreled over the kingdoms of God and of Hell.

28. Therefore God said: *Jacob* I have loved, and *Esau* I have hated; and from this arises <term>election by grace</term> <note>original: "Gnaden-wahl"; the theological concept of God's sovereign choice or predestination, which Böhme interprets as a struggle between different spiritual "principles" within the human soul.</note> over the children who cling to Him...

Böhme uses this as a metaphor for the grace Christ provides to make the soul's cleansing possible.</note>, so that we might step out of the Wrath immediately in our childhood. Thus the **noble stone** <note>original: "edle Stein"; Böhme's term for the divine spark or the Christ-spirit within the soul, which transforms the "base metal" of human nature into "spiritual gold."</note> is then despised. Wherever a person is seen who carries this stone, he must be their fool. The cause is this: they have the **serpent’s wit** <note>original: "Schlangen Wiß"; the cunning, intellectual cleverness of the fallen world, as opposed to divine wisdom.</note>, and he who has the stone is without such wit, being just like a child. His play in this world consists of grief, need, contempt, and misery; but it stands written: *They go indeed hence and weep, but they carry noble seed.* <note>A reference to Psalm 126:6.</note> **Eternity** is better than a short moment of eye-pleasure followed by eternal mourning.

37. Because we then recognize such things and know in the ground of our being that we lie caught in a heavy **imprisonment**, we wish to reveal here that very ground along with the imprisonment, to see if anyone might wish to see what he actually is. We will not speak **historically** <note>original: "Hiſtoriſch"; for Böhme, "historical" knowledge is rote learning or academic study that lacks personal, spiritual experience.</note>, but rather of what we recognize in ourselves, in body and soul, and what we see at the foundation of the world. We shall speak out of our own **Light**, which we have received out of grace, and not out of a conceit or opinion where we must doubt whether it be true.

38. It is said: what the eyes see, the heart believes. It is good to see with one’s own eyes; but he who sees with foreign eyes always doubts whether the spirit be right or false. Therefore, it is good to have the **noble stone**, for it gives certainty and points out the false **magicians** <note>original: "Magos"; Böhme uses this to describe those who claim spiritual authority without true insight.</note>, who are merely **book-learned wise men** <note>original: "Hiſtorien Magi"; those who know the "history" or the letter of the law but not its spirit.</note>. They parade about with their histories like a harlot who wants to be called a virgin, yet is already with child...

## Cap. 7. Of Man.

<margin>Cap. 7.</margin>
...pregnant. Thus they are pregnant with **darkness** and **wrath**, and yet they cry out constantly: "Here is the Church! Here is Christ! Everyone run here!" Yes, indeed, run to the **Whore of Babylon** <note>original: "Huren zu Babel"; Böhme's term for the corrupt, institutionalized religious systems that prioritize power and dogma over inner spiritual truth.</note>, who is pregnant with **pride**; attend her at her childbed, so that she can fatten her **bastard brat** <note>original: "Hurenbalck"; literally a whore's brat, referring here to the false doctrines and worldly structures born of spiritual adultery.</note> and satisfy her glittering, stinking pride. They are like whores who, when told they are whores, will not endure it, but curse and blaspheme. Likewise, when the **Spirit of Truth** confronts them, they cry out: "O heretic, heretic! Bring fire here! O run, flee everyone, for the devil is there!" Thus they name the Spirit of God, because they do not know Him.

39. We write this not out of a desire to mock them, for we recognize the great misery of our **imprisonment** <note>Böhme frequently refers to the physical body and the fallen state of the soul as a "prison" or "captivity."</note>; rather, we do so because the simple person hangs so much upon their words and believes everything the devil pours out in wrath. We write so that everyone should enter into themselves and test whether it be the truth, and not zeal in blindness with wrath and envy, without knowing the foundation or the truth.

40. Thus we have enough experience to know that often the **Holy Spirit** is called a devil, and the devil a good spirit, and this often happens unknowingly. For the **hypocrites** <term>Gleißner: literally "those who glisten"; people who put on a show of holiness but lack inner truth</term> fill people's ears with fair speeches and pull the **Scriptures** according to their own desires. O, it is a most terrifying vice! That God's Spirit must be disgraced by the **image of God** <note>original: "Bildnuß Gottes"; the human being, who was created to reflect God but has become a vessel for the "serpent."</note>; though we do not say that the *image* does it, but rather the **serpent** within the image. ### Chapter 7. Of Man.

<margin>Chapter 7.</margin>
...that it has two spirits / one is the outflow of the heat / and the other is the outflow of the light : Now, the heat belongs to nature / and the light belongs to the eternal freedom outside of nature / for nature does not grasp the light. <note>This is a reference to the Gospel of John 1:5, "the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not understood it."</note>

43. So understand us then concerning the two wills in God : One is of nature / which is not called God / and yet belongs to God / for it is wrathful / fierce / prickly / consuming / pulling everything to itself and devouring / always flowing out over the light / and yet unable to reach it / just as fire does : The higher it flies / the higher the light is / and they may well be called two *Principles* <note>original: "Principia"; Böhme's term for the fundamental planes of reality (Darkness/Fire vs. Light/Love).</note> : For the light desires substantiality <term>Wesentheit: In Böhme’s writing, this refers to a spiritual "body" or "essence" that gives form to the divine light.</term> / and holds substantiality / and does not consume it / and the fire desires to devour everything / and to make it into a nothingness / and when it has not done that / it becomes a darkness. Therefore God moved himself in the light of gentleness <term>Sanfftmuth: The yielding, soft quality of divine love that pacifies the harsh "fire" of the first principle.</term> / and put on gentleness / so that the light has a substantiality / which is water or, in the *holy ternary* <note>original: "ternario sancto"; refers to the divine manifestation or the three-fold nature of the spiritual world.</note>, the Water-spirit / which keeps the fire captive / so that the fire is thus a darkness / and is not recognized / unless it be enkindled; And it stands within itself in hunger in the eternal darkness / and is thus a constant desiring.

44. From such an original source come the devils / for it is the wrath of God : and everything that is false and evil / originates itself thus from this *matrix* <note>original: "matrice"; the womb or creative source from which all things are born.</note>. and all creatures of this world / be it heaven / stars / earth / and whatever it may be / and everything has a twofold quality <term>Quahl: A pun on the German "Qual" (torment/pain) and "Quelle" (source/quality), suggesting that the very source-spring of life contains a tension or "torment."</term> / as fire and water? # The IX. Chapter.

## On the Threefold Life, and on the impulse and entire governance of man in this world: to be highly considered.

1. It has been shown to me what the Devil has in mind, and how he intends to cover up these worthy and high writings. Therefore, take heed, you children of GOD; do not believe the Sophists <term>Sophists: here, a derogatory term for academic theologians or legalistic scholars who rely on intellectual logic rather than spiritual experience</term> too much, who cry out, "O heretic, heretic, bring on the fire!" It is not the voice of the Holy Spirit, but that of the Antichrist and the Dragon. For these writings shall powerfully reveal the Devil's smoke-hole <note>original: "Rauchloch"; likely referring to the source of his deceptions or the vent of the abyss</note>. And not only this, but they present the Whore of Babylon <term>Whore of Babylon: a biblical figure from the Book of Revelation, used by Böhme to symbolize the corruption and spiritual adultery of the institutional church</term> quite clearly, like a harlot in the pillory.

2. Therefore, because the people of the spirit of this world are only concerned with their bellies—so that they do not wish to lose their honor and property, but would much rather lose God and the Kingdom of Heaven—we shall be persecuted by the Whore through the impulse of the Devil. Therefore, take heed, you children of God, and do not look upon the high things that possess power, but consider the welfare of your souls: we leave this to you as a parting word <note>original: "zur letze"; a final admonition or legacy</note>.

3. Christ says: No one lights a light and puts it under a bench or a bushel <term>bushel: a measuring container for grain; used here in reference to the Parable of the Lamp to describe hiding spiritual truth</term>, but sets it upon the table, so that all who are in the house may see by it. We should also do this, and not bury our talent <term>talent: original "Pfundt" (pound), referring to the Parable of the Pounds in Luke 19, signifying the spiritual gifts and insights entrusted to a person by God</term>—which has been given to us at a high and dear cost—in the earth. # Of the Threefold Life Chap. 9

...[it] is given of the Sower, where the Devil sows weeds among the seed: As this now is in the human <term>mind <note>original: "Gemühte"; refers to the soul's disposition, encompassing thoughts, feelings, and will</note></term>, so it is also in the spirit of this world.

10. You should know that all evil weeds, such as thorns and thistles, as well as snakes, toads, evil beasts, and worms, have their origin from the <term>Fierce Matrix <note>original: "Grimmen Matrice"; in Böhme’s cosmology, the "Matrix" is the womb or generative ground of nature. The "Fierce" or "Wrathful" aspect refers to the harsh, dark quality of nature that exists when separated from God's light</note></term>. Within it, at the time of creation, everything—both evil and good—came forth, each according to its kind and property. In all things there is evil and good: and the Kingdom of Wrath has completely formed itself within; therefore, the fruit is both evil and good, and Adam was not supposed to eat from it.

11. I show you this by the fruits of the earth, how all things evil and good stand mixed together, and each has its usefulness, the evil as well as the good. All things exist for God’s miraculous work and serve the spirit of this world. What one spoils, the other heals, and that too is a miracle.

12. Furthermore, we see the <term>Great Mystery <note>original: "Mysterium Magnum"; the hidden, spiritual source or "chaos" from which the physical world was manifested</note></term> in the trees; though they are also diverse and mixed, we still recognize the Paradisiacal form: for they bear their fruits upon branches, and the fruit is something other than the tree. The tree is bitter, and the fruits are sweet. And we give you this to understand: that even today we have Paradisiacal trees and fruits, if only the curse did not dwell within them. Paradise has fled from them, and the fruit is now altogether such food as the apple was, from which Eve ate her death.

If we wish to know what a human being is, and why there is such a great difference among people—so that one does not act like another, and one is different in form and shape from another—then we must take up and consider the innermost **Ground** <note>original: "Grund"; refers to the essential, underlying reality or foundation of a being</note> of the process of becoming human <note>original: "Menschwerdung"; often refers to the Incarnation of Christ, but here Böhme applies it to the spiritual and physical formation of every human being</note>; therein we find everything.

<margin>How one reborn in God may search into the three Principles. What kind of **governance** such a person has within themselves in the image of the spirit and body.</margin>
34. For when a person is born again in God, so that they stand in the Light, and when such a person begins to search from their **original state** <note>original: "Urstande"; the primordial source or beginning</note>, then the spirit of the soul searches into all three Principles to see what it is in each of them. For we then recognize this, and cannot say otherwise, but that in the image of the spirit and also of the body, we have only one kind of **governance** <note>original: "Regiment"; the internal rule, order, or dominant force governing a person's life</note> within us across all three Principles.

<margin>What drives the spirit and body. Whichever Principle a person follows, those are the works they perform.</margin>
35. And according to whichever Principle gains the **upper hand** in a person—so that the person aligns themselves with it through their will—it is according to that Principle that they perform their works; the other Principles merely cling to them without sufficient power.

<margin>What the image is in its Ground. How humans are sown into the **Matrix**.</margin>

Now look and consider yourself: what comes before this? Nothing but a longing will of man and woman toward their union; and yet the fruit is not always desired, as one sees in the examples of prostitutes and rogues, and indeed also in marriage.

### Chapter 9. Of Man.

...contraction and cold are a form <note>original: "gestalt"; in Böhme’s system, these are the seven fundamental qualities or "source-spirits" that constitute all reality</note> and spirit at the Center, which shuts up the abyss <note>original: "Abgrund"; the bottomless, infinite void of eternity before creation</note> and creates darkness in the depth. Thus, that which is contracted stands like a wheel over against **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturno"; the first source-spirit, representing cold, contraction, and the "dark" impression</note> and is called the **Moon**, because of its property, though to write of this in full would take too much space.

# Of the Threefold Life Chapter 9

...nus <note>This is the conclusion of the previous page's final sentence regarding the spirit of Venus.</note>: For it is the gentleness of the outward nature and creates Love: For it is the desirer of the other five qualities <note>original: "Gestalten"; Böhme’s term for the seven fundamental properties or spirits of nature.</note>.

80. For every quality winds itself inward and desires the **freedom of God**, which is gentle, still, and like a **Nothing**—and yet it is everything. And when they then obtain the gentleness, which also produces **water**, the water is thick and resembles **darkness**. This water desires **light** and longs for the light exceedingly, and it becomes pregnant, so that the gentleness (as **Venus** <note>original: "Venus"; the fifth source-spirit, representing the desire for light and the power of love.</note>) has its own shine above all stars in the firmament; for the desire catches the light.

81. Now the light is without substance <note>original: "ohne Wesen"; meaning it is purely spiritual and lacks a physical or essential "body" at this stage.</note>, being only still and gentle. It desires life and spirit, and yet it can draw no life or spirit out of the water and the gentleness.

82. 83. Now this would be unstable and would pass away as often as the wheel turned once. And even if it lasted a long time, it would endure for an age <term>seculum</term> <note>original: "seculum"; typically meaning a century, but here referring to a full orbital cycle of Saturn (approx. 29 years).</note> of twenty-nine years. Therefore, the seven qualities desire **Fire**—a fire that remains. For without fire, the heart has no life. And the heart catches fire, and the fire is fierce and consuming, and it consumes all seven qualities of the center <term>Centri</term> <note>original: "Centri"; the core point of manifestation where nature's forces are balanced.</note> along with their substance.

#### [Of the] Threefold Life Chapter 9.

...[than] we recognize and see here. Therefore, understand us correctly; we wish to make this difficult concept easier for you; see and take note of it.

102. The entire **governance** <note>original: Regiment; refers to the ordered rule or system of nature</note> of this world in every kind of life comes from the **stars** <note>original: Gestirne; refers to the constellations and celestial influences</note>, both evil and good; for they are also the cause by which the four elements—namely fire, air, water, and earth—are awakened; otherwise, everything in this world would be still.

103. Thus you see primarily in the **Seven Planets** the supreme governance, for they are the governance of the spirit, and it is twofold: they possess the governance of the **Tincture** <note>original: Tinctur; in Böhme’s thought, this is the spiritualizing medicinal power or "quintessence" that brings life and light to matter</note>, as the fire-life, and also the air-governance, as the water-life.

104. The three planets above the **Sun** <note>In Böhme’s cosmology, these are Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note> conduct the fire-life and governance along with the Sun. And the three below the Sun <note>Venus, Mercury, and the Moon</note> are the outflow of the fire’s *Tincture*, and are a sinking-down; they conduct the governance of light along with the Sun and possess the female gender, for they have the essence of the **Matrix** <note>original: Matricis; the "womb" or generative source of physical nature</note>, while those above have the *Tincture* of the Matrix.

105. The *Tincture* holds the soul, and the lower **Matrix of Venus** <note>original: Matrix Veneris</note> holds the spirit. Thus the higher desires the lower, and the lower desires the higher; and it is indeed one body, for the **Sun** <note>original: Sol</note> is the heart and possesses the luster of the majesty of this **Principle** <note>original: Principii; Böhme divides reality into three "Principles": the dark fire-world, the light-world, and the outer physical world</note>. Thus you understand the two genders, male and female.

106. The man is the head and has within himself the supreme governance with the fire’s *Tincture*, and he has the soul within his *Tincture*; he desires **Venus** <note>original: Venerem; the feminine aspect or planetary force</note> as the physical **Matrix** <note>original: Matricem</note>,

### Chapter 9. Of Man.

<margin>Chapter 9.</margin>
...when the soul desires to have a spirit and desires to have a body; and the **Matrix** <note>original: Matrix; refers to the womb or the generative, formative power of nature</note> of woman possesses that. And the lower **governance** <note>original: Regiment</note> is the feminine, and her governance resides in the **Moon**: For **the Sun** <note>original: ☉ Sol</note> gives her the heart, and **Venus** gives the **Tincture** <note>In Böhme’s thought, the "Tincture" is the spiritualizing life-essence that brings qualities to matter</note>. However, she does not possess a fiery Tincture, but rather a watery one. Therefore, the Sun gives the spirit of air, and her Tincture does not consist of heat.

107. For this reason, the man must govern her, for the Tincture of fire is the sharp testing of all beings. **Mercury** is the awakener of her Tincture, which is why they are talkative <note>Böhme attributes "talkativeness" to the astrological influence of Mercury, the planet of communication, acting upon the feminine watery element</note>. And the Moon possesses her **Matrix** <note>original: Matricem</note>; it is composed of all the planets and is fearful of the Earth; therefore, it hurries so quickly and takes power into its wheel from all the planets and stars wherever it can.

108. It intensely desires **the Sun** <note>original: Solis</note>, and therefore it draws the Sun's radiance to itself. And just as the Moon longs for the Sun—because it is of an earthly nature and desires a heavenly heart—so too does the feminine Matrix long for the heart of the man, and for his Tincture, as if for the soul; for the soul is the eternal good.

109. Thus nature now longs for the Eternal and would gladly be free of vanity. And so, the intense desire originates in the feminine and masculine genders of all **creatures**, so that one longs to mingle with the other. For the physical body does not understand this, nor does the spirit of air; only the two Tinctures—masculine and feminine—understand it.

110. For a beast does not know what it does; only the Tinctures know it, and they drive the creatures to act so.

12. For he does not dwell in the external, but in the <term>Centrum Naturæ</term> <note>Center of Nature. In Böhme's thought, this is the internal point where spiritual forces originate before manifesting outwardly.</note>, and he proceeds from within the Deity out into the external, opening up an image according to himself—understand this as being according to the **Center of Nature**.

13. We have told you before how the **Wheel of outer Nature** <note>original: "Radt der äussern Natur." ### Of the Threefold Life, Chapter 11.

<margin>
How a repentant sinner, who wishes to enter the Christian community or the Body of Christ, is to be received; how sins are forgiven in God's stead, and how he becomes a partaker of the Body.
</margin>
...repentant sinner comes, who wishes to enter the community <note>original: "Gemeyne"; refers to the spiritual congregation or the "communion of saints"</note> of Christ and who desires Christ, the community should receive him. For Christ has received him, and so in Christ we are all one Body. And just as one limb supports and loves the other, so we should receive one another; we should take the poor, converted sinner into our community and announce to him the forgiveness of sins in God's stead. We should lay our hands upon him and make him a partaker of our body and fellowship; thus our spirit and power will also rest upon him, as was seen with the Apostles.

<margin>
48. Here the power to forgive sins is given to us, as we lead them into God, through Christ to the Father; how he should properly sink himself into our love within our will.

49. How we are the community and Bride of Christ, whom He loves; and that what we do, Christ does in us, and God in Christ.
</margin>
47. When we receive him into Christ’s community, he is our brother. When we say, "Your sins are forgiven," then they are indeed drowned <note>Böhme uses the word "ersäuffet" (drowned) to emphasize the total destruction of the old, sinful nature in the "blood" of Christ</note> in Christ's death and blood, and he becomes a member of Him. We do not take the sins away from him ourselves; rather, Christ in us drowns them through our faith and his faith in His blood. When we lay our hands upon him and pray over him, we press with our will—which is in God—into his will. We lead him within our own will, as if in one body in Christ, to the Father. His will becomes our will, for he gives himself through Christ into the Bride <note>The "Bride of Christ" here represents the collective spiritual unity of the believers</note>—that is, into our will, which is also God's will. We rightly take him into our love and into our will, and we sink ourselves with him through Christ into God. In this way, we forgive him his sins. For we are the community and Bride of Christ, whom He loves: and whatever we do, Christ does it in us, and God in Christ.
